Since you last pressed Play - The Royal Court
Details: Advanced > What changed since I last pressed Play.
The Royal Court is a fast, light mod manager for Crusader Kings III. This short tour shows the features that save you the most trouble.
Your playsets are saved as Paradox Launcher playset files, so nothing is locked in.
No installer and no browser. The program goes online only when you press Updates.
It never changes your mod files. It reads them to find problems.
You can open this tour again at any time from Advanced > Show the quick tour again.
If your mods do not appear, type your Crusader Kings III folder at the bottom (the folder that contains "mod") and press Save folder.
A playset is a list of mods with an order. The order matters: when two mods change the same thing, the one lower in the list wins.
Tick a mod to turn it on or off. Every change is saved at once.
Drag rows, or use Up and Down, to change the order. Hold Ctrl or Shift to select several mods and move them together.
Use New, Duplicate, Rename and Delete for your playsets. Duplicate one before you experiment.
Click a column header to sort the view. The Notes column flags missing mods, mods made for an older game and conflicts.
The filter box next to the magnifier finds a mod by name as you type.
Press Auto Sort and the program proposes a better load order. Nothing changes until you look at the preview and press Apply.
Dependencies go first, then libraries, overhauls, content, graphics, interface, translations and patches.
Total conversions load first, and well-known mods such as Rise and Fall are placed where their authors say.
Right-click a mod to lock it so Auto Sort never moves it, or to correct its type.
Not happy with the result? Undo order puts the list back as it was.
Sorted something wrongly? Advanced > Report a sort problem copies the details so the known-mods list can be fixed.
Conflicts shows where mods collide, before you spend an evening in a broken game.
By mod pair or by file: mods that ship the same file. The mod loaded last usually wins.
By definition: mods that define the same trait, event, define or localization key.
Base game: mods that replace a file of the game itself. The game never merges those.
Double-click a file to see every mod that ships it and who wins. Right-click a row to let one mod win; the order is saved and checked again.
Every conflict has a severity (High, Medium, Low). Type high, medium or low in the filter box to see only those.
Play starts Crusader Kings III directly with the playset you selected, without the Paradox Launcher.
Steam must be running. The program writes your playset into the game's dlc_load.json first.
Your own dlc_load.json is kept next to it as dlc_load.json.rc-original.
Your playset is backed up automatically at startup and before Auto Sort.
Advanced has Back up now, Restore from a backup and Open backups folder.
Game launch options for each playset (for example -debug_mode) are under Advanced.
Three helpers read the game's own files and tell you where to look. They only read; they never change anything.
Crash helper: after a crash it says what kind of crash it was and which of your mods the last log messages point at.
Game log: every error and warning of the game, grouped by the mod it comes from, with a copy button for the mod's author.
What changed since I last pressed Play: mods that updated, mods made for an older game, mods turned on or off, a game update.
The status line at the bottom tells you when the game crashed or when something changed.
These helpers are in the Advanced menu.
A few things that make the program yours.
Export > Copy a share code turns a whole playset into one line of text. Import > Paste a share code builds it again for a friend.
The language button in the top bar switches the program between eleven languages at once.
The sun and moon switch changes between the dark and the light look.
Updates checks GitHub when you press it and can update the program in place.
That is the tour. Enjoy your court!

A crash with no recognised cause

This is the most common crash with mods. It is usually a script or data file the game cannot handle: a mod that is out of date for this game version, two mods that overwrite the same files, or a mod loaded in the wrong order. Check the suspects below, then try turning off the most recently added or updated mods first.
A big playset on a long game can use more memory than the computer has. Close other programs, turn off graphics-heavy and map mods first, and restart the game now and then in a long campaign.
This is almost always a mod that makes events or effects call each other forever. Look at the suspects below, and at mods that changed recently.
This points at the graphics driver or card rather than a script mod. Update the graphics driver, and turn off mods that add many or large textures, 3D models or shaders.
The game found data that does not make sense. A mod that is out of date for this game version is the usual reason.
This usually means damaged game files or an unstable overclock. Verify the game files in Steam.
A mod gave the game a value of zero where it must not. Check the suspects below.
The crash files do not say what went wrong. The suspects below come from what the game wrote to its log just before it stopped.
